q: Mind is the forerunner of all actions. Speak or act with a pure mind, and happiness follows like a shadow that never departs.
s: Dhammapada 1.1–2, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion does not break through a well-trained mind.
s: Dhammapada 1.14, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if already dead.
s: Dhammapada 2.21, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: By effort, heedfulness, restraint, and self-mastery, let the wise make for themselves an island which no flood overwhelms.
s: Dhammapada 2.25, trans. John Ross Carter

q: As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought.
s: Dhammapada 3.33, trans. F. Max Müller

q: The mind moves far and works alone, without a body, hidden in a cave. Those who subdue this mind are freed from Māra's bonds.
s: Dhammapada 3.37, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: Whatever an enemy might do to an enemy, or a foe to a foe, a misdirected mind creates worse harm to oneself.
s: Dhammapada 3.42, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: As a bee takes nectar without harming the flower, its color, or its scent, so should the sage move through a village.
s: Dhammapada 4.49, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Even one who shows you where you have gone wrong, as if pointing out buried treasure, is someone to cherish.
s: Dhammapada 6.76, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Irrigators guide water; fletchers straighten arrows; carpenters bend wood; the wise discipline themselves.
s: Dhammapada 6.80, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not shaken by praise or blame.
s: Dhammapada 6.81, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: The wise, concentrated, taking delight in the calm of renunciation — like a lake, deep, clear, and still.
s: Dhammapada 6.82, trans. Narada Thera

q: Like the Himalayan peaks, the good shine from afar. The unwholesome are not seen, like arrows shot in the night.
s: Dhammapada 6.84, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: Like the earth, the trained one takes no offense. Like a threshold, he is steady. Like a lake free from mud, he is clear.
s: Dhammapada 7.95, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Better than a thousand hollow words is one word that brings peace.
s: Dhammapada 8.100, trans. Thomas Byrom

q: One who conquers oneself is greater than one who conquers a thousand in battle.
s: Dhammapada 8.103, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: Better is one day of seeing the arising and passing of all things than a hundred years lived without that seeing.
s: Dhammapada 8.111, trans. Narada Thera

q: Don't think lightly of evil, saying 'it will not come to me.' A water pot is filled by falling drops; even so, the fool fills himself with evil, gathered little by little.
s: Dhammapada 9.121, trans. Narada Thera

q: Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the wise man, gathering it little by little, fills himself with good.
s: Dhammapada 9.122, trans. Narada Thera

q: A carpenter bends wood; a fletcher straightens arrows; the wise shape themselves.
s: Dhammapada 10.145, trans. F. Max Müller

q: See this painted puppet, this body with its wounds, afflicted and full of longing. In it there is no lasting power, no permanence.
s: Dhammapada 11.147, trans. Narada Thera

q: This body is like a clay vessel — frail, brief, easily broken. One who knows this does not quarrel.
s: Dhammapada 11.148, trans. Buddharakkhita

q: If you hold yourself dear, guard yourself well. The wise should keep watch through every one of the three watches of the night.
s: Dhammapada 12.157, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: First establish yourself in what is good, then instruct others. Such a wise person will not be stained.
s: Dhammapada 12.158, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: This world is blind. Few here see clearly. Like birds escaping a net, few go to heaven.
s: Dhammapada 13.174, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Not to do any evil, to cultivate good, to purify one's mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
s: Dhammapada 14.183, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: Patience is the highest austerity. Nibbāna, say the Buddhas, is supreme. One who harms others is no renunciant.
s: Dhammapada 14.184, trans. Buddharakkhita

q: Health is the foremost gain. Contentment is the foremost wealth. Trust is the foremost relative. Nibbāna is the foremost ease.
s: Dhammapada 15.203–204, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Having known the taste of solitude and of the peace of tranquility, one is free from fear and free from wrong, drinking the joy of the Dhamma.
s: Dhammapada 15.205, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: Conquer anger by non-anger; conquer evil by good; conquer miserliness by generosity; conquer a liar by truth.
s: Dhammapada 17.223, trans. Narada Thera

q: You are now like a withered leaf. The messengers of death have arrived. You stand at the journey's threshold, and have no provision for the road.
s: Dhammapada 18.235, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: As a skilled smith removes dross from silver, purifying it little by little, moment to moment, so the wise man removes impurities from himself.
s: Dhammapada 18.239, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: Iron, born of the earth, is destroyed by its own rust; even so, the over-strict ascetic is destroyed by his own deeds.
s: Dhammapada 18.240, trans. Narada Thera

q: All conditioned things are impermanent. When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purity.
s: Dhammapada 20.277, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: All conditioned things are suffering. When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purity.
s: Dhammapada 20.278, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: All phenomena are without self. When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purity.
s: Dhammapada 20.279, trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita

q: The gift of Dhamma surpasses all gifts. The taste of Dhamma surpasses all tastes. Delight in Dhamma surpasses all delights.
s: Dhammapada 24.354, trans. Narada Thera

q: One who can remain undisturbed when touched by the vicissitudes of life — without sorrow, without elation, taintless — this is the highest blessing.
s: Sutta Nipāta 2.4 (Maṅgala Sutta) v.10, trans. K.R. Norman

q: From whatever way the wind blows, the sage is not disturbed. Like a great rock firmly planted, he remains.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.1 (Uraga Sutta) v.6, trans. K.R. Norman

q: As a snake casts off its worn-out skin, so one who has abandoned all that is past moves on.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.1 (Uraga Sutta) v.1, trans. K.R. Norman

q: Do not ask about lineage; ask about conduct. From any wood, fire is born. From any family, a person of resolute character can arise.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.7 (Vasala Sutta) v.21, trans. K.R. Norman

q: As a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so too toward all living beings one should cultivate a boundless mind.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.8 (Metta Sutta) v.7, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The householder and the forest-dweller, the ox-driver and the wheel-wright — all who practice rightly reach the further shore.
s: Sutta Nipāta 2.14 (Dhammika Sutta) v.20, trans. K.R. Norman

q: The one who clings to nothing, who neither praises nor blames — who is like the moon on a cloudless night — that one I call a brahmin.
s: Sutta Nipāta 4.14 (Tuvaṭaka Sutta) v.14, trans. K.R. Norman

q: Seeing the danger in attachment, and freedom in letting go, I will live without clinging. This is the practice.
s: Sutta Nipāta 4.5 (Metta Sutta commentary), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: As a flame blown by the wind goes out and is not reckoned as existing anywhere, so too the sage released from name and form simply goes out.
s: Sutta Nipāta 5.1074 (Parayanavagga), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: I ask you about the island, the great sage, about the further shore — speak of that place where one does not grieve.
s: Sutta Nipāta 5.1093 (Parayanavagga), trans. K.R. Norman

q: Train yourself: in what is seen, there will be just the seen; in what is heard, just the heard; in what is sensed, just the sensed; in what is cognized, just the cognized.
s: Udāna 1.10 (Bāhiya Sutta), trans. John Ireland

q: There is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned. If there were not, there would be no escape from the born, the become, the made, the conditioned.
s: Udāna 8.3 (Paṭhama Nibbāna Paṭisaṃyutta), trans. John Ireland

q: Wondrous! Wondrous! All living beings are endowed with the Tathāgata's wisdom and virtue, but because of delusion and clinging they cannot realize it.
s: Avataṃsaka Sūtra, ch. 1 (Bodhisattva birth cry, traditional rendering)

q: Do not depend on others; make of yourself a lamp. Make of the Dhamma your lamp. Seek no other refuge.
s: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16.2.26), trans. Maurice Walshe

q: Work out your salvation with diligence. All conditioned things are impermanent.
s: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16.6.7), last words of the Buddha, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: There are these five ways of removing annoyance. One should think: 'This is how it is; this is how it must be dealt with.' Thus annoyance is removed and practice proceeds.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 21 (Kakacūpama Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Even a well-made raft must be left behind once the far shore is reached. The teaching is like a raft — for crossing over, not for clinging to.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 22 (Alagaddūpama Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation. Knowing this, the wise do not mourn what has passed.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 26 (Ariyapariyesanā Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Form is like a lump of foam; feeling like a water bubble; perception like a mirage; volitions like a banana tree trunk; consciousness like a conjurer's trick.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95 (Phena Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: As a pot of water placed in fire gradually grows warm, so too the mind, repeatedly applied to contemplation, gradually becomes clear.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.204, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The lute string that is tuned too tightly will break; tuned too loosely, it will not produce sound. The middle tension produces music.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.55 (Soṇa Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: If one's actions were all done with care, not one of them would leave a stain. The fool, acting carelessly, is never free.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.100 (Kusīta Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: As a goldsmith tests gold by rubbing, cutting, and burning, so should you examine my words before accepting them.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.65 (Kālāma Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: There are four ways of attending to things: attending to what is beneficial, avoiding what is harmful, undertaking what is good, and releasing what is not.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.77, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Whatever arises dependent on conditions: that is empty. Whatever is empty is subject to arising. These two truths are not opposed.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.15 (Kaccānagotta Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: One who knows what is timely, what is true, what is gentle, connected with the goal, and spoken with a loving heart — that one speaks beautifully.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.198, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: As the great earth is not troubled by what is placed upon it, pleasant or unpleasant, so the trained mind takes in both without disturbance.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.218, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: A person of integrity: what he says, he does; what he commits to, he fulfils. He is reliable as a balance.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.73, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The wise craftsman finishes his work and then stands back. The heavens and the earth spring from his work, yet he does not interfere.
s: Jātaka 316 (Mahāumagga Jātaka), prose commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Even the longest journey begins with a single step placed with clear intention.
s: Jātaka 1 (Apannaka Jātaka), teaching verse, trans. Robert Chalmers

q: The fool rushes to finish; the wise one takes time to measure. Both finish, but only one builds what stands.
s: Jātaka 31 (Kulāvaka Jātaka), verse 4, trans. H.T. Francis

q: A thousand small repairs make a great house; a thousand small acts of care make a great character.
s: Jātaka 107 (Salittaka Jātaka), verse 2, trans. H.T. Francis

q: As a potter does not force the clay but works with its nature, so the wise do not force the mind but work with its nature.
s: Jātaka 107 (Salittaka Jātaka), prose frame, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The grain of the timber is already there. The carpenter only reveals what was waiting within.
s: Jātaka 178 (Daddara Jātaka), prose frame, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Even a stone that has been in the river a hundred years is not wet through. Even so, the wise person lives in the world without being soaked by it.
s: Jātaka 240 (Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka), verse 3, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Watchfulness protects: watch the ox as it grazes, watch the mind as it rests — for what is unguarded wanders into harm.
s: Jātaka 221 (Kukkuṭa Jātaka), verse 1, trans. H.T. Francis

q: One who has crossed a difficult pass does not forget the path. One who has found freedom does not forget the teaching that showed it.
s: Jātaka 269 (Sattubhasta Jātaka), verse 2, trans. Robert Chalmers

q: A craftsman who knows the nature of one hundred timbers does not hesitate before a timber he has not seen before.
s: Jātaka 360 (Saṅkha Jātaka), prose frame, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The mountain does not resist the seasons; the sea does not resist the rivers. Patience receives all things without loss.
s: Jātaka 522 (Samuddavāṇija Jātaka), verse 1, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Truth is the highest virtue; truth is the foundation of the world. Speak truth above all things.
s: Jātaka 537 (Mahāsutasoma Jātaka), verse 6, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Even the longest night has a dawn. Even the deepest forest has a path. Begin, and the way will become clear.
s: Jātaka 510 (Mahājanaka Jātaka), verse 2, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Rough stone, worked day by day with patience, becomes smooth. Rough character, worked day by day with practice, becomes refined.
s: Jātaka 301 (Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka), verse 1, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The wise person neither hastens what is not yet ripe nor delays what is ready. This is the art of living.
s: Jātaka 310 (Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka), prose frame, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Do not let a day pass in which you have not applied yourself to something worthy. The day unused is already spent.
s: Jātaka 480 (Bhuridatta Jātaka), verse 11, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The craftsman's mark remains when the craftsman is gone. Let your mark be worthy.
s: Jātaka 222 (Kiṃpakka Jātaka), verse 1, trans. H.T. Francis

q: A well-made thing speaks without words. It says: I was made by a patient hand.
s: Jātaka 112 (Mahā-Sīlava Jātaka), verse 4, trans. Robert Chalmers

q: Beginners begin; those who continue, excel. Those who finish and begin again become masters.
s: Jātaka 404 (Dabbhapuppha Jātaka), verse 3, trans. H.T. Francis

q: I had made many pots, many bowls. Yet the finest vessel I made was a vessel for holding what cannot be held.
s: Therīgāthā 13.1 (Ambapālī Therī), trans. Charles Hallisey

q: I have sat in the grass until it flattened, and risen before the dew dried. This is how I came to know the mind.
s: Theragāthā 18.1 (Mahākassapa Thera), trans. K.R. Norman

q: The weaver said to the cloth: you are not my work; you are the meeting of every thread. So too the mind is the meeting of every moment.
s: Theragāthā 6.4 (Adhimutta Thera), verse 9, trans. K.R. Norman

q: Do not be satisfied with small attainments, thinking 'enough has been done.' Long is the path; great is the fruit. Do not stop here.
s: Theragāthā 1.92 (Māluṅkyaputta Thera), trans. K.R. Norman

q: Young in the teaching, devoted to the path — this one is like new rice: full of promise and not yet tasted.
s: Theragāthā 1.103, trans. K.R. Norman

q: See this body: aged, diseased, a nest of aches — and yet the one who looks is free from none of it. Where is the looker?
s: Therīgāthā 6.1 (Cittā Therī), trans. Charles Hallisey

q: I left behind the golden bracelets, the beautiful clothes, the painted cosmetics. I washed it all away in the stream of the path.
s: Therīgāthā 6.2 (Vimalā Therī), trans. K.R. Norman

q: In my old age I took the robe; in my old age I took the bowl. I was like a newly sharpened blade — late, but keen.
s: Therīgāthā 13.2 (Rohiṇī Therī), trans. Charles Hallisey

q: In the dead of night, when the fire was low, I understood: no outside force shapes the mind. The mind makes itself.
s: Theragāthā 20.1 (Adhimutta Thera), verse 14, trans. K.R. Norman

q: I am a carpenter's daughter; I know the grain of wood, the weight of a mallet, the smell of fresh sawdust. The Dhamma, I learned, has the same texture as a well-cut joint.
s: Therīgāthā 7.1 (Nandā Therī), commentary tradition, trans. K.R. Norman

q: As a skilled carpenter, having made the mortise and tenon fit, does not then wonder if the joint will hold, so the trained meditator does not then wonder if the mind is capable.
s: Milindapañha 2.2.9, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: The mind is like a well-tempered sword: it must be kept sharp by use, but not overworked until it becomes brittle.
s: Milindapañha 3.7.1, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: A bowl fashioned without care, however fine the clay, will crack at first use. A mind trained without mindfulness, however bright by nature, will fail at first test.
s: Milindapañha 3.4.5, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: Just as a lamp does not choose where it gives light, so compassion does not choose its objects.
s: Milindapañha 4.1.7, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: As the ship-builder bends the timber to the curve, knowing the shape before the wood has moved — so the meditator shapes the mind with a vision already held.
s: Milindapañha 5.1.1, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: A mind in deep meditation is like a lake in calm weather: every fish can be seen, every stone on the bottom is visible.
s: Milindapañha 3.2.11, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: Just as the ocean has one taste — the taste of salt — so the Dhamma has one taste — the taste of liberation.
s: Udāna 5.5 (commentary on Pācittiya rules), Vinaya tradition, trans. I.B. Horner

q: As fire does not think 'I will burn this,' and yet burns, so the compassionate one does not think 'I will help this one' — and yet helps.
s: Milindapañha 7.4.2, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: Just as a good physician does not give medicine before diagnosis, a good teacher does not give teaching before listening.
s: Milindapañha 2.1.3, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: As a goldsmith purifies gold by heating, hammering, and refining, not all at once but by degrees, so the meditator purifies the mind by degrees.
s: Visuddhimagga I.11, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Virtue is the soil; concentration is the rain; wisdom is the flower. Without the soil and the rain, the flower cannot grow.
s: Visuddhimagga I.1, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: As a lamp burns in a windless place and does not flicker — so the mind in deep concentration rests, unmoving.
s: Visuddhimagga IV.34, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Just as an expert dyer, knowing each cloth requires its own preparation, prepares each before dyeing, so the meditator prepares each mind-moment before attending.
s: Visuddhimagga XIV.5, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The builder of a great house labors long in the hidden foundations where no one sees. So too, the meditator labors long in the hidden ground of virtue.
s: Visuddhimagga II.3, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: As a patient jeweler does not rush the setting but fits each stone to its place, so the skilled teacher does not rush the instruction but fits each teaching to its student.
s: Visuddhimagga IX.12, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Whatever is made by the hands must first be made in the mind. Whatever is shaped in the mind must first be shaped in the heart.
s: Visuddhimagga XIV.1, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Bodhidharma sat before Emperor Wu. 'What is the highest truth of the holy teaching?' 'Vast emptiness, nothing holy.' 'Who stands before me?' 'I do not know.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 1, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said: Mu.
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 1, trans. Robert Aitken

q: Before thinking good and evil, what is your original face?
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 23, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: Yunmen said: 'Every day is a good day.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 6, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Dongshan asked: 'When cold and heat come, how do you avoid them?' The monk said: 'Go where there is no cold or heat.' Dongshan said: 'Where is there no cold or heat?'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 43, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Nanquan said: 'Ordinary mind is the Way.'
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 19, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: A monk asked Zhaozhou: 'Does a newborn baby have the sixth consciousness?' Zhaozhou said: 'Throwing a ball on swift water.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 80, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Yantou said: 'Whatever arises, no grasping; whatever passes, no chasing. This is the whole practice.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 51, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Deshan said: 'If you have understood, you go; if you have not, you also go.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 28, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Xuefeng said: 'The whole earth is you. The whole earth is me. When I lift a grain of rice, it is the whole earth.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 5, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Zhaozhou's cypress tree stands in the garden. The monk asked: 'What is the meaning of Bodhidharma coming from the West?' Zhaozhou said: 'The cypress tree in the garden.'
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 37, trans. Robert Aitken

q: Yunmen held up his staff and said: 'The staff has transformed into a dragon and swallowed the universe. Where are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 60, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Baizhang was asked: 'What is the extraordinary thing?' He said: 'Sitting alone on Daxiong Peak.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 26, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: A monk asked Mazu: 'What is Buddha?' Mazu said: 'This very mind is Buddha.'
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 30, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: Later a monk asked Mazu: 'What is Buddha?' Mazu said: 'Neither mind, nor Buddha.'
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 33, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: A monk asked Dongshan: 'What is Buddha?' Dongshan said: 'Three pounds of flax.'
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 18, trans. Robert Aitken

q: Juzhi Osho raised one finger whenever he was asked a question about Zen. That was all he ever did.
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 3, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: Lingzhao was asked about the nature of the bright and clear. She said: 'When the master makes a fan and asks what it is — that is the bright and clear.'
s: Book of Serenity, Case 24, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Guishan asked Yangshan: 'Through the day, through the year, through the age — how do you pass?' Yangshan said: 'As always.'
s: Book of Serenity, Case 20, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Zhaozhou asked Nanquan: 'What is the Way?' Nanquan said: 'Your ordinary mind — that is the Way.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 19, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Dongshan asked Yunmen: 'When cold and heat come, how does one escape?' Yunmen said: 'Why not go where there is no cold or heat?' Dongshan said: 'What is that place?'
s: Book of Serenity, Case 52, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Linji said: 'Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down — everything is the Buddha's activity.'
s: Record of Linji (Línjì Yùlù), trans. Burton Watson

q: Linji said: 'If you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him.' This means: do not cling even to enlightenment.
s: Record of Linji (Línjì Yùlù), trans. Burton Watson

q: Linji said: 'The student of today cannot identify the disease. It is this: lack of confidence in oneself.'
s: Record of Linji (Línjì Yùlù), trans. Burton Watson

q: Huang Po said: 'The foolish reject what they see, not what they think. The wise reject what they think, not what they see.'
s: The Zen Teaching of Huang Po (Huangbo Duanji), trans. John Blofeld

q: Huang Po said: 'To study the Buddha is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self.'
s: The Zen Teaching of Huang Po (Huangbo Duanji), trans. John Blofeld

q: Mazu said: 'This very mind, just as it is — that is the Buddha.' Nothing added, nothing removed.
s: Extensive Record of Mazu Daoyi, trans. Cheng Chien Bhikshu

q: Baizhang said: 'A day without work is a day without eating.' He kept his hoe until the day he died.
s: Record of Baizhang (Bǎizhàng Qīngguī), trans. Thomas Cleary

q: When Baizhang's disciples hid his tools to keep him from working in old age, he refused to eat until his tools were returned.
s: Record of Baizhang (Bǎizhàng Qīngguī), trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Zhaozhou said: 'Have you eaten your rice gruel? Then go wash your bowl.' This is the whole teaching.
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 7, trans. Robert Aitken

q: Guishan said to Yangshan: 'All day you do my work; what do you give me in return?' Yangshan drew a circle in the air. Guishan said: 'That is correct.'
s: Book of Serenity, Case 67, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Study is not learning; learning is not understanding; understanding is not realization. But without study, the rest cannot begin.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Bendōwa (Wholeheartedly Engaged in the Way), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: To study the Way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be verified by all things.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan (Actualizing the Fundamental Point), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Robert Aitken

q: When you walk in the mist, though you may not notice, your robe becomes damp. When you practice in the Way, though you may not notice, you become the Way.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: A fish swims in water and however far it swims, there is no end to the water. A bird flies through the sky and however far it flies, there is no end to the sky.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Masao Abe

q: Practice does not wait for understanding. Begin now, and understanding will arrive.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Bendōwa, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: Being Buddha is not a destination; it is what you already are, lived fully, moment by moment.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Shōji (Birth and Death), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: Those who are greatly enlightened about delusion are Buddhas; those who are greatly deluded about enlightenment are sentient beings.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Robert Aitken

q: Mountains are mountains; rivers are rivers. After study, mountains are no longer mountains, rivers no longer rivers. After realization, mountains are again mountains, rivers again rivers.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Sansuikyō (Mountains and Waters Sutra), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Carl Bielefeldt

q: Mountains walk. Waters flow. This is not metaphor; this is how things are.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Sansuikyō, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Carl Bielefeldt

q: A great master does not copy the ancients. A great master finds what the ancients were seeking.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Zazenshin (Acupuncture Needle of Zazen), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: In the kitchen, there is no separation between the cook's mind and the soup. The soup is the mind; the mind is the soup.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Thomas Wright

q: Handle even a single leaf of a green vegetable as if it were the golden body of the Buddha.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Edward Brown

q: When preparing rice, do not view it as merely doing work. When washing rice, do not think of it as merely washing. When cooking, do not think of it as merely cooking.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Thomas Wright

q: The cook who moves through the kitchen with no wasted motion — this is the movement of a thousand years of attention.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Edward Brown

q: Give your full attention to the work of the moment. The work of the moment is the work of a lifetime.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Do not use the food of the monastery for your own stomach; use your stomach for the food of the monastery. This is giving.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Thomas Wright

q: The six tastes — bitter, sour, sweet, salty, light, heavy — all appear in the kitchen. The cook who knows them all knows more than most monks know of doctrine.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun (Instructions for the Cook), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Edward Brown

q: When you rise in the morning, wash your face; when you sit, sit. Do not let your attention be elsewhere while your hands are here.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Shōji, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: The entire universe is the dharma body of the self. The entire dharma body is the self of the universe. Therefore, even a blade of grass is Buddha.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Busshō (Buddha-nature), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Masao Abe

q: Being present, fully present, is the whole teaching. Anything else is commentary.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, commentary tradition

q: To be verified by all things is to remove the barrier between one's own body and mind and the bodies and minds of others.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: At this moment, the whole earth, the sun, the moon, and the stars are all the mind of zazen.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Zazenshin, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Realization does not shatter delusion as a hammer breaks stone. Realization is like the sun that makes mist dissolve without violence.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, commentary tradition

q: Time is not a container in which things happen. Things are time; time is things. The moment of making is the moment of being made.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Uji (The Time Being), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: All of time is present in this moment. This moment contains the whole of time. Work, then, as if eternity depended on this cut.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Uji, Dōgen Zenji, trans. David Loy

q: The Platform Sutra says: without cleansing, even the mirror cannot reflect. But if there was never a mirror, what is there to cleanse?
s: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch (Liuzu Tanjing), Huineng, trans. Philip Yampolsky

q: Original nature is pure. If you know your original nature, you yourself are Buddha.
s: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, Huineng, trans. Philip Yampolsky

q: When the eighth-century master Huineng was a woodcutter, he heard a man recite: 'Dwelling nowhere, let the mind arise.' At that moment he was enlightened.
s: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, ch. 1, trans. Philip Yampolsky

q: Good friends, the Dharma does not need east, west, north, or south. Your own nature, without obstruction — that is the place of practice.
s: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, ch. 2, trans. Philip Yampolsky

q: A person who practices Dhyana in his sitting does not see the mistakes of the world. Though the sky is above and the earth below, he does not see distance.
s: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, ch. 5, trans. Philip Yampolsky

q: Nothing is holy; vast emptiness — this was Bodhidharma's answer. Why then do we sweep the steps each morning? Because the steps are dusty.
s: Chan teaching, attributed to Bodhidharma's lineage, traditional

q: The founder of the school of no-mind says: cook your rice, sweep your floor, go to sleep. Nothing hidden; nothing extra.
s: Recorded Sayings of the Chan Masters (Zutangji), trans. Albert Welter

q: Huanglong asked three questions: 'What is the hand that holds things? What is the foot that walks the road? How do you see the Ch'an master clearly?' No one answered for forty years.
s: Blue Cliff Record, commentary on Case 35, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: The sage does not compete, and therefore no one can compete with him.
s: Attributed to Sengzhao (374–414 CE), Zhào Lùn (Treatises of Seng-chao), trans. Walter Liebenthal

q: All phenomena arise from the mind. The mind is like a great artist painting the world.
s: Avataṃsaka Sūtra (Flower Garland Sutra), ch. 20, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: One who has realized the nature of mind sees clearly that the universe is a pure land. The pure land is not elsewhere.
s: Vimalakīrti Sūtra, ch. 1, trans. Robert Thurman

q: Vimalakirti fell silent. Manjushri said: 'Well done. Not a letter, not a syllable — that is truly entering non-duality.'
s: Vimalakīrti Sūtra, ch. 9, trans. Robert Thurman

q: Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form.
s: Heart Sūtra (Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya Sūtra), trans. Thich Nhat Hanh

q: When the Bodhisattva of Deep Wisdom practiced the perfection of wisdom, she saw that the five aggregates are empty, and crossed beyond all suffering.
s: Heart Sūtra, trans. Red Pine

q: The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma like rain falling: it falls equally on all plants. But each plant receives it according to its own nature.
s: Lotus Sūtra, ch. 5 (The Parable of the Medicinal Plants), trans. Leon Hurvitz

q: This Dharma is not something acquired; it is recognized. It was never not here.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 2, trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: The mind does not dwell in the past, does not dwell in the future, does not dwell in the present. Dwelling nowhere, it arises.
s: Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra (Diamond Sutra), ch. 10, trans. Red Pine

q: Like a star, a defective eye, a lamp, a mirage, a dewdrop, a bubble, a dream, a lightning flash, a cloud — see all conditioned phenomena as thus.
s: Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā), closing verse, trans. Red Pine

q: For one who sees, this world is not a solid place but a web of arising — each thread dependent on every other thread, none more real than the rest.
s: Avataṃsaka Sūtra, ch. 30 (Indra's Net commentary), trans. Thomas Cleary

q: The bodhisattva acts without any thought of reward; she does not count what she gives, nor remember what she has received.
s: Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines), ch. 1, trans. Edward Conze

q: Taking care with every task, you are like the artisan who knows that the seen work reflects the unseen practice.
s: Mahāvastu (Great Story), vol. I, ch. 4, trans. J.J. Jones

q: Nāgārjuna said: whatever is dependently arisen is empty. Whatever is empty is dependently arisen. These two are not different views — they are one recognition.
s: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.18, Nāgārjuna, trans. Jay Garfield

q: Nothing arises from itself; nothing arises from another; nothing arises from both; nothing arises from neither. Therefore nothing arises at all — in the absolute sense.
s: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 1.1, Nāgārjuna, trans. Jay Garfield

q: If things existed by their own nature, then change would be impossible. What we observe — change, growth, decay — proves things do not exist in that way.
s: Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 15.8, Nāgārjuna, trans. Jay Garfield

q: The person who sees impermanence clearly does not cling; the person who does not cling does not suffer; the person who does not suffer is free.
s: Ratnāvalī (Precious Garland) I.35, Nāgārjuna, trans. Jeffrey Hopkins

q: Carefully, carefully — so that no harm is done; patiently, patiently — so that no haste intrudes. This is the way of the bodhisattva in all work.
s: Ratnāvalī (Precious Garland) II.17, Nāgārjuna, trans. Jeffrey Hopkins

q: If you wish to protect yourself and others, practice equanimity. For the expert in equanimity, there is no pain that cannot be borne.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.120, Śāntideva, trans. Kate Crosby

q: All the unhappiness in the world arises from seeking happiness for oneself alone. All the happiness in the world arises from seeking happiness for others.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 8.129, Śāntideva, trans. Stephen Batchelor

q: Just as the hand protects the foot from a thorn without thinking 'that is not my hand,' so the bodhisattva protects others without thinking 'that is not myself.'
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 8.120–121, Śāntideva, trans. Kate Crosby

q: Anger destroys in one instant the good accumulated over thousands of years. There is no sin equal to hatred, no practice equal to patience.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.1–2, Śāntideva, trans. Stephen Batchelor

q: If something can be remedied, why be unhappy about it? And if it cannot be remedied, what is the use of being unhappy?
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.10, Śāntideva, trans. Kate Crosby

q: As long as space endures, as long as beings remain, so long may I also remain to dispel the misery of the world.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 10.55, Śāntideva, trans. Stephen Batchelor

q: Do not correct the faults of others when you yourself are driven by pride. First put out the fire in your own house.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 5.19, Śāntideva, trans. Kate Crosby

q: One thought of anger toward a bodhisattva destroys the merit of a hundred kalpas. Guard the mind — of all things to guard, none is more important.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 5.1–2, Śāntideva, trans. Stephen Batchelor

q: Work faithfully; let the work show what the worker was. No signature is needed — a well-made thing bears witness to itself.
s: Atiśa, Bodhipathapradīpa (Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment), verse 37, trans. Richard Sherburne

q: My religion is kindness.
s: Attributed to the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, in various teachings

q: On the frozen mountain, with no fire and no shelter, I heated myself by the fire of my own nature. This is the practice of inner heat.
s: Milarepa, Songs of Milarepa (Mgur 'bum), ch. 3, trans. Garma C.C. Chang

q: Do not be proud of your realization; do not be ashamed of your delusion. Both are the mind at work, and the mind does not need your opinion of it.
s: Milarepa, Songs of Milarepa, ch. 14, trans. Garma C.C. Chang

q: I sing without knowing what to sing; I teach without knowing what to teach. This not-knowing is itself the teaching.
s: Milarepa, Songs of Milarepa, ch. 7, trans. Garma C.C. Chang

q: When I worked in the fields, the field was my teacher. When I sat in the cave, the cave was my teacher. Everything teaches, if you are a student.
s: Milarepa, Songs of Milarepa, ch. 22, trans. Garma C.C. Chang

q: The practitioner who does not work is like a lamp without oil. Eventually it goes out.
s: Milarepa, Hundred Thousand Songs (Mgur 'bum), commentary tradition, trans. Chang

q: Guru Rinpoche said: my religion is no distraction. My religion is total presence.
s: Padmasambhava, Samantabhadra's Wish-Fulfilling Prayer, trans. Erik Pema Kunsang

q: The nature of mind is like the sky: naturally pure, naturally bright, naturally vast. Clouds appear and pass; the sky does not become cloudy.
s: Padmasambhava, Bardo Tödröl (Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State), ch. 1, trans. Chogyam Trungpa

q: If you realize the nature of your own mind, you are already a Buddha. If you do not realize it, you are still a Buddha — you just do not know it yet.
s: Padmasambhava, Bardo Tödröl, ch. 3, trans. Chogyam Trungpa

q: The recognition of one's own nature takes no time. The recognition cannot be practiced — it can only be arrived at.
s: Tilopa, Ganges Mahamudra, trans. Ken McLeod

q: Cut the root of a tree, and the leaves will wither. Cut the root of mind, and samsara falls.
s: Tilopa, Ganges Mahamudra, trans. Ken McLeod

q: Don't recall. Don't imagine. Don't think. Don't examine. Don't control. Rest.
s: Tilopa, Ganges Mahamudra, trans. Ken McLeod

q: Naropa had learned all the words. Tilopa said: learning all the words has given you a box — now break the box.
s: Life of Naropa (Nāropā'i rnam thar), traditional account, trans. Herbert Guenther

q: A fine arrow is not made quickly. A fine student is not made quickly. But the arrow, once made, flies true forever.
s: Sakya Pandita, Legs bshad rin po che'i gter (Treasury of Aphoristic Jewels), trans. John Davenport

q: Examine the teacher as you would examine gold: by rubbing, cutting, and melting. Do not trust on the basis of reputation.
s: Atisha, Bodhipathapradīpa, commentary, trans. Richard Sherburne

q: Do everything you do with a clean heart. If the heart is clean, even the roughest work is pure.
s: Patrul Rinpoche, Words of My Perfect Teacher (Kunzang Lama'i Zhalung), trans. Padmakara Translation Group

q: Impermanence is not sad news; it is the news that change is possible, that practice is possible, that liberation is possible.
s: Patrul Rinpoche, Words of My Perfect Teacher, ch. 1, trans. Padmakara Translation Group

q: The teachings say: death is certain; the time of death is uncertain. Act accordingly.
s: Patrul Rinpoche, Words of My Perfect Teacher, ch. 2, trans. Padmakara Translation Group

q: Do not waste a single day. You may not have the next one.
s: Patrul Rinpoche, Words of My Perfect Teacher, ch. 3, trans. Padmakara Translation Group

q: The greatest obstacle to practice is distraction. The greatest support for practice is remembering death.
s: Patrul Rinpoche, Words of My Perfect Teacher, ch. 5, trans. Padmakara Translation Group

q: Machig Labdrön said: confess your hidden faults; approach what you find repulsive; help those you think you cannot help; go to places that frighten you. This is the practice of cutting through.
s: Machig Labdrön, Gcod kyi chos skor (Chöd Teachings), trans. Jerome Edou

q: Whatever arises in your experience — offer it. Let the hungry spirits have your flesh. Let the demons have your pride. Then see what remains.
s: Machig Labdrön, Mahamudra Gcod, trans. Jerome Edou

q: Tsongkhapa said: the root of all good qualities is finding a reliable guide and following them well. Do not rush this; do not mistake cleverness for guidance.
s: Tsongkhapa, Lam Rim Chenmo (Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path), vol. 1, trans. Lamrim Chenmo Translation Committee

q: The mind habituated to virtue acts virtuously without effort. This is the fruit of long practice.
s: Tsongkhapa, Lam Rim Chenmo, vol. 2, trans. Lamrim Chenmo Translation Committee

q: Candrakīrti said: do not be attached to the view of emptiness any more than to a view of permanence. The raft must be abandoned at the far shore.
s: Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra (Entry into the Middle Way), ch. 6, trans. C.W. Huntington Jr.

q: When a craftsman truly understands the material, the material itself shows the way. This is not magic; this is attention.
s: Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa, ch. 4 (commentary tradition), trans. Leo Pruden

q: The five aggregates are like a burden; the person who carries them is like the bearer. Wisdom arises when the bearer knows what it is carrying.
s: Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa 5.1, trans. Leo Pruden

q: You build a house; the house does not build you. But over time, the house you build comes to build you. This is karma.
s: Vasubandhu, Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa (Treatise Proving Karma), trans. Leo Pruden

q: Do not grasp at the concept of emptiness, lest you fall into the extreme of annihilation. Do not grasp at the concept of existence, lest you fall into the extreme of eternalism.
s: Aryadeva, Catuḥśataka (Four Hundred Verses) 8.15, trans. Karen Lang

q: The student who works diligently at the beginning of study, and then relaxes, is like a craftsman who levels the foundation and then builds the walls crooked.
s: Dharmakīrti, Pramāṇavārttika (Commentary on Valid Cognition), ch. 2, verse 143, trans. Tom Tillemans

q: Valid cognition is the root of all successful action, just as a correct blueprint is the root of a well-built house.
s: Dharmakīrti, Pramāṇavārttika, ch. 1, verse 1, trans. Tom Tillemans

q: Ajahn Chah said: if you let go a little, you will have a little peace. If you let go a lot, you will have a lot of peace. If you let go completely, you will have complete peace.
s: Ajahn Chah, A Still Forest Pool, trans. Jack Kornfield

q: Ajahn Chah said: looking for the Buddha outside yourself is like looking at your own reflection in a mirror and asking where your face is.
s: Ajahn Chah, A Tree in a Forest (Dhamma talks), trans. Paul Breiter

q: If you are not yet at peace, it is because the wanting is still there. The wanting is the noise; the peace was always underneath.
s: Ajahn Chah, Food for the Heart, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Ajahn Mun said: the Dhamma is always being taught — by the wind, by the rain, by the way fire burns. We are students whether we know it or not.
s: Ajahn Mun, Muttodaya (The Heart Released), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: Mahasi Sayadaw said: note 'rising, falling' — the breath rises, falls, rises, falls. In each noting, a small freedom. In a thousand notings, a great one.
s: Mahasi Sayadaw, Practical Insight Meditation, trans. U Pe Thin

q: Shunryu Suzuki said: in beginner's mind there are many possibilities; in the expert's mind there are few.
s: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Weatherhill

q: Shunryu Suzuki said: the most important thing is to find out what is the most important thing.
s: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Weatherhill

q: Each moment, each step — these are not preparations for your life. They are your life.
s: Shunryu Suzuki, Not Always So, HarperCollins

q: The teaching is not a set of directions; it is a set of lights. You must carry it yourself.
s: Nyanaponika Thera, The Heart of Buddhist Meditation, Weiser

q: When we pay attention, we are giving the highest gift we have to give: our presence.
s: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Miracle of Mindfulness, Beacon Press

q: Washing the dishes is washing the Buddha. There is no hierarchy of holy and mundane.
s: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Miracle of Mindfulness, Beacon Press

q: The present moment is the only moment available to us, and it is the door to all moments.
s: Thich Nhat Hanh, Peace is Every Step, Bantam Books

q: The lotus grows from the mud. The skilled practitioner grows from difficulty.
s: Thich Nhat Hanh, Touching Peace, Parallax Press

q: When you are cutting the wood, cut the wood. When you are carrying it, carry it. This instruction contains the entire Path.
s: Seungsahn (Seungsahn Haengwon), Only Don't Know, Primary Point Press

q: Before thinking: what is this? Before speaking: what is this? Before acting: what is this? This question, kept alive, is the practice.
s: Seungsahn, Dropping Ashes on the Buddha, Grove Press

q: Ananda asked the Buddha: 'Is good friendship half the holy life?' The Buddha replied: 'Say not so, Ananda. Good friendship is the whole of the holy life.'
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.18 (Upaddha Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: If one practices well, one should not take credit; the Dhamma should take credit. The teacher is only a finger pointing at the moon.
s: Itivuttaka 111, trans. John Ireland

q: The monk who has few wishes, who is content, who lives in seclusion — that one does not tremble before the world.
s: Itivuttaka 17 (Dve Dhammā), trans. John Ireland

q: As a lamp feeds on oil, so a person feeds on what they give attention to. Attend to the good; feed on the good.
s: Itivuttaka 26, trans. John Ireland

q: One thing, when done and cultivated, leads to great benefit: recollection of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha — and your own good actions.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.296, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The skilled woodworker selects only seasoned wood; the skilled mind selects only wholesome thoughts. This is the beginning of craft.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.1, commentary tradition, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: What is made with mindfulness holds together; what is made with distraction falls apart sooner or later.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 44 (Cūḷavedalla Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: A monk was asked: 'What is the mark of wisdom?' He said: 'Doing only what needs to be done, and doing it well.'
s: Majjhima Nikāya 139 (Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta), commentary tradition, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The dharma is not a wall to be broken through by force. It is a path to be walked with steady attention.
s: Digha Nikāya 2 (Sāmaññaphala Sutta), commentary, trans. Maurice Walshe

q: As a smith shapes hot iron — patiently, not too fast, not too slow — so the disciple shapes the mind.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.100 (Paṃsudhovaka Sutta, Goldsmith Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: A thought of ill-will burns the thinker first. Do not keep such fire in your own house.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.60, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: There is no fire like passion, no snare like delusion, no river like craving, no ocean like existence.
s: Dhammapada 18.251, trans. Narada Thera

q: Easy it is to see the faults of others, hard it is to see one's own faults. Like chaff one winnows others' faults, but one's own one hides.
s: Dhammapada 18.252, trans. Buddharakkhita

q: There is no meditation for one who lacks wisdom. There is no wisdom for one who lacks meditation. One in whom both are present is near to Nibbāna.
s: Dhammapada 25.372, trans. Narada Thera

q: As a hollow reed is filled by water, so a hollow mind is filled by whatever it is placed near. Fill it well.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.143, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The monk stands at the edge of the forest in the early morning. The birds begin to sound. He does not move. This is his practice.
s: Theragāthā 16.7 (Adhimutta's solitude verses), trans. K.R. Norman

q: In the first watch of the night, I recalled ten thousand former births. In the second watch, I saw ten thousand deaths. In the third watch, I understood: it is the clinging, not the birth or death, that is the problem.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 36 (Mahāsaccaka Sutta), night of enlightenment account, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The Blessed One said: whatever you frequently think and ponder upon, that will become the inclination of your mind. Train the inclination well.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 19 (Dvedhāvitakka Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: One who reads a hundred books has a head full of words. One who practices a single teaching has a heart full of wisdom. Both are needed; neither alone is enough.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.102, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Even a beautiful verse, recited a thousand times but not practiced, is as a lovely flower without fragrance.
s: Dhammapada 4.51, trans. Narada Thera

q: But even a single verse, practiced and lived by, bears fruit forever.
s: Dhammapada 4.52, trans. Narada Thera

q: The one who is not swept away by the current of praise, who is not stopped by the current of blame — that one stands on firm ground.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.6, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Three things cannot long remain hidden: the sun, the moon, and the truth.
s: Dhammapada, commentary tradition attributed to the Buddha

q: The teaching is not mine to give; you already have it. I only remind you of what you already know.
s: Digha Nikāya 16.3.50, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta commentary, trans. Maurice Walshe

q: When there is no self, who suffers? When there is no other, who is harmed? Seeing this fully is seeing the empty nature of conflict.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 72 (Aggivacchagotta Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: In giving, one loses nothing and gains much. In hoarding, one seems to gain but loses the use of what is hoarded.
s: Jātaka 547 (Vessantara Jātaka), verse 68, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: An open hand is never empty. A closed hand holds only what is already in it.
s: Jātaka 501 (Sivi Jātaka), verse 12, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Light from one candle lights another without diminishing itself. So it is with teaching.
s: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta commentary tradition, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: Delight in non-violence. Delight in restraint. Cultivate goodwill toward all who live. This is joy that does not diminish.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.3 (Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, Rhinoceros Horn Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Go alone as the rhinoceros horn. Go undistracted. Go not seeking the praise of the crowd.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.3 (Khaggavisāṇa Sutta), trans. K.R. Norman

q: In solitude you hear the mind. In company you hear the world. Both are teachers; neither is the final word.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.3, commentary, trans. K.R. Norman

q: Like bamboo that bends in the storm but does not break, the patient practitioner bends before difficulty and rises again afterward.
s: Jātaka 455 (Canda Jātaka), verse 4, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The weaver's shuttle, the farmer's plow, the monk's needle — all are tools of the same essential work: to make something out of nothing.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.4, commentary tradition, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Shakyamuni was a carpenter's kinsman. He knew: a well-fitted joint needs no glue. A well-trained mind needs no force.
s: Lalitavistara Sūtra, ch. 11 (Royal Training section), trans. Gwendolyn Bays

q: The teaching says: do not add; do not subtract. What is needed is already here.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 3 (Mahāmati's Questions), trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: Just as fire does not ask for fuel before burning, wisdom does not ask for permission before illuminating.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 26 (Ariyapariyesanā Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The kite flies high because the string holds it. Cut the string and it falls. The string is the precepts.
s: Visuddhimagga I.39, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Precepts without wisdom are a house without light. Wisdom without precepts is a flame without shelter. Each needs the other.
s: Visuddhimagga I.1 (commentary on the opening verse), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: A person without virtue is a person without tools. They wish to build but have nothing to build with.
s: Visuddhimagga I.7, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Just as the sun does not distinguish between the clean and unclean in giving its light, so compassion does not distinguish between the worthy and unworthy.
s: Visuddhimagga IX.8, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: What you do in the early morning, before the world asks anything of you — this is who you truly are.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 4 (Bhayabherava Sutta), commentary tradition, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Sit. Be still. Not to get something — just to be. The getting will take care of itself.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Zazenshin, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: The cook who prepares the morning gruel with the same devotion as the evening feast — that one has understood non-discrimination.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: A Zen master was asked what happens after death. He said: 'I don't know.' The student said: 'But you are a Zen master!' He said: 'Yes, but not a dead one.'
s: Gateless Gate commentary tradition, attributed to Dizang Guichen

q: A monk asked: 'What is the one thing that, if known, all things are known?' The master picked up his robe and walked away. This is the teaching.
s: Book of Serenity, Case 1, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Lingyun saw peach blossoms and was enlightened. He wrote: 'For thirty years I sought a sword-master. How many times the leaves fell and the boughs bloomed anew. Then I saw peach blossoms once — and now I have no doubts at all.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 41, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Xiangyan swept the ground and a pebble struck a bamboo. At the sound, he was enlightened. He said: 'One stroke has made me forget all my learning. No more practice needed; just living the original way.'
s: Gateless Gate, Case 5 commentary, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: Yunmen said: 'The world is wide and vast. Why do you put on your robe at the sound of the bell?' No answer is the answer.
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 16, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: The first lesson of the craftsman is: measure twice, cut once. The first lesson of the meditator is: look twice, speak once. The first lesson of the sage is: hear twice, conclude never.
s: Sayings of Zhaozhou (Zhaozhoulu), trans. James Green

q: Asked about the Way, the master said nothing. Asked again, he said nothing. Asked a third time, he said: 'You are asking about the Way with your mouth.'
s: Recorded Sayings of the Chan Masters (Zutangji), vol. 4, trans. Albert Welter

q: The student who completes a beautiful piece of calligraphy and then destroys it — that student understands non-attachment to results.
s: Dōgen Zenji, Extensive Record (Eihei Kōroku), vol. 1, trans. Taigen Dan Leighton

q: You do not polish a tile to make a mirror. You do not sit in meditation to become a Buddha. You sit because sitting is your nature.
s: Mazu Daoyi, encounter with Nanyue Huairang, from Jingde Chuandeng Lu, trans. Andy Ferguson

q: Huike stood in the snow and cut off his arm to show Bodhidharma his sincerity. Bodhidharma said: 'Bring me your mind, and I will put it at rest.' Huike said: 'I cannot find it.' Bodhidharma said: 'Done.'
s: Gateless Gate, Case 41, trans. Robert Aitken

q: A carpenter who has never made a mistake has never tried anything difficult. Difficulty is the teacher the textbook cannot replace.
s: Jātaka 175 (Āsaṅka Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The jar that holds water does not proclaim itself. The teaching that holds truth does not proclaim itself. But both are known by use.
s: Sutta Nipāta 3.12 (Dvayatānupassanā Sutta), trans. K.R. Norman

q: Contemplate the nature of all things made: they are assembled from parts; they will disassemble; they were never, finally, the fixed thing they appeared to be.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 131 (Bhaddekaratta Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Let the past go — it cannot be remade. Let the future go — it has not yet come. Hold the present — only here is where the work is done.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 131 (Bhaddekaratta Sutta), verse 1, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: The monk who lives in the forest hears the rain on the leaves and does not wish for shelter. This is not indifference; this is the ease of one who is completely present.
s: Theragāthā 2.2 (Nāgasamāla Thera), trans. K.R. Norman

q: They asked Ananda: 'What should we do after the Buddha has gone?' He said: 'Make of the teaching your refuge. Make of yourself your refuge. Let nothing else be your refuge.'
s: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16.2.26), trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: The best place to meditate is wherever you are right now.
s: Theragāthā 1.22 (Adhimutta Thera), trans. K.R. Norman

q: There is a place where no making occurs, no unmaking occurs, no standing still occurs. That place is the goal. Everything else is the path.
s: Udāna 8.1, trans. John Ireland

q: When the cloth is woven, the weaver disappears into the cloth. This is the great art: to vanish completely into the work.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, commentary tradition

q: Right view is the prerequisite of all the other factors of the path — as the first light of dawn precedes the rising sun.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 117 (Mahācattārīsaka Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Not by birth is one a noble; not by birth is one an outcast. By action one is a noble; by action one is an outcast.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.7 (Vasala Sutta), verse 21, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The practitioner handles the world as a skilled potter handles clay — with firm but gentle hands that know the material completely.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.100 (Goldsmith Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Zen master Bankei said: the unborn Buddha-mind is bright, illuminating all things by its own light. It was never not shining.
s: Bankei Yōtaku, Zen and the Art of Dying (Bankei Zenji Hōgo), trans. Norman Waddell

q: Bankei said: you are already in the unborn; you are already complete. Your searching is like a person with eyes wide open, looking for their eyes.
s: Bankei Yōtaku, The Unborn: The Life and Teaching of Zen Master Bankei, trans. Norman Waddell

q: Hakuin said: 'This very place is the lotus land; this very body, the Buddha.' Meditate here, now, in this form, in this moment.
s: Hakuin Ekaku, Song of Zazen (Zazen Wasan), trans. Robert Aitken

q: From the beginning, not a thing has ever been lacking. The student walks for years to find what was never missing.
s: Hakuin Ekaku, Song of Zazen, trans. Senzaki Nyogen

q: A student asked the master: 'Where does the path lead?' The master said: 'Where does the road in front of your house lead?'
s: Recorded Sayings of Chan Masters (Zutangji), traditional exchange, trans. Albert Welter

q: Work done with care honors the material, honors the maker, and honors the one who receives it. This is the three-fold gift of good craft.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The perfect piece is not the piece without flaws. It is the piece in which the flaws have been understood and answered.
s: Jātaka 404 (Dabbhapuppha Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: In the Zen tradition, cleaning the floor is a teaching. Cleaning the mind is also cleaning the floor. They are the same motion.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary tradition, trans. Edward Brown

q: If you hear the Dhamma and do not practice it, you are like a man who reads a map but never makes the journey.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.160, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The teaching that cannot be stated in a single sentence is not complete. The teaching that can be stated in a single sentence is not complete. This is the teaching.
s: Vimalakīrti Sūtra, ch. 5 (The Dharma Door of Non-Duality), commentary, trans. Robert Thurman

q: Everything that is made eventually breaks, falls, wears away, or is abandoned. This is not tragedy — it is the nature of making. Make anyway.
s: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16), closing commentary tradition, trans. Maurice Walshe

q: A monk who knows how to wait, knows how to begin. Patience and beginning are the same skill, seen from opposite ends.
s: Jātaka 240 (Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The teacher said: 'Go sharpen your tools.' The student sharpened the tools and returned. The teacher said: 'Now sharpen your attention.' The student worked another forty years.
s: Zen teaching story, traditional (no primary source)

q: The hardest thing in any craft is knowing when it is finished. The second hardest thing is knowing when to begin.
s: Jātaka 316 (Mahāumagga Jātaka), teaching commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: If you do the work, the work will teach you. Books can only tell you what others learned from the work.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.66 (Kālāma Sutta), commentary tradition, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: There are those who hear the sound of the chisel and learn carpentry. There are those who take up the chisel and never hear the sound. The former become masters.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 65 (Bhaddāli Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The careful person makes many things. The careless person makes many broken things. The wise person makes fewer things, more perfectly.
s: Jātaka 112 (Mahā-Sīlava Jātaka), verse 8, trans. Robert Chalmers

q: Shāriputra said: 'I am only a learner.' But the learner who knows they are learning is already ahead of the one who thinks they are done.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 74 (Dīghānakha Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Do not say: 'I have no time for practice.' Say instead: 'I have not yet understood what practice is.' When you understand, time appears.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.71, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: What you build in a hurry you will repair at leisure. What you repair at leisure you will learn to build rightly.
s: Jātaka 407 (Kaṭṭhabharī Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The bricklayer who lays each brick carefully, checking the level each time, builds walls that stand a hundred years. This is the only secret of good building.
s: Jātaka 358 (Saṅkhapāla Jātaka), prose frame, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: When the mind is settled, even a difficult thing becomes possible. When the mind is scattered, even a simple thing becomes difficult.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.6, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: You study a hundred forms of the craft and then, one day, you forget all the forms and your hands know what to do. That day is the beginning of mastery.
s: Zen painting tradition (zenga), attributed to Sengai Gibon (1750–1837), traditional

q: The world is burning with the fire of desire, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. What are you building in a burning world? Build a place where the fire does not reach.
s: Ādittapariyāya Sutta (SN 35.28, 'Fire Sermon'), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: The fire was the teacher of teachers. Sit near it long enough and you learn: nothing holds its shape forever, and that is what makes everything possible.
s: Sutta Nipāta 1.1 (Uraga Sutta), teaching commentary

q: In the furnace, every impurity is revealed. In practice, every hidden fault is revealed. This is why the furnace is revered, and why practice is revered.
s: Dhammapada 18.239, commentary tradition

q: A student of Dōgen asked how to proceed in practice. Dōgen said: 'Start where you are. Use what you have. Do what you can. This is already more than enough.'
s: Shōbōgenzō: Shōji, commentary tradition, Dōgen Zenji

q: Bankei asked his disciples: 'Right now, who is listening?' No one answered. 'Exactly,' he said. 'That one — that is the unborn Buddha-mind.'
s: Bankei Yōtaku, Zen Sermons (Bankei Zenji Hōgo), trans. Norman Waddell

q: The student said: 'I practice every day, but I do not improve.' The master said: 'You are improving. You just cannot see it yet. Practice is always ahead of the practitioner.'
s: Dōgen Zenji, Eihei Kōroku (Extensive Record), vol. 3, trans. Taigen Dan Leighton

q: The one who knows the wood grain, the one who knows the water current, the one who knows the mind's inclination — all are students of the same teacher.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.143 (extended commentary), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: There is no shortcut to a well-cut tenon. There is no shortcut to a well-trained mind. Both require the accumulated weight of a thousand correct motions.
s: Milindapañha 2.1.5, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: Even the Tathāgata worked. He made robes; he repaired his bowl; he swept his cell. Do not imagine that great realization exempts one from great work.
s: Vinaya Piṭaka, Cullavagga V.5, trans. I.B. Horner

q: The cloth that lasts is woven tightly. The mind that holds is trained thoroughly. There is no other method.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 78 (Samaṇamaṇḍikā Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Before nirvana, chop wood; carry water. After nirvana, chop wood; carry water. The action is the same. The one performing it has changed completely.
s: Zen teaching, traditional (widely attributed)

q: Huangbo said: the foolish are afraid of the mind. The wise enter it freely. Only the one who enters freely is safe.
s: The Zen Teaching of Huang Po (Huangbo Duanji), trans. John Blofeld

q: To know the self fully is to be free of the self. The self, fully known, cannot hold you.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Robert Aitken

q: Two monks argued about a flag: is the flag moving or the wind? Huineng said: neither the flag nor the wind — only your mind is moving.
s: Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, ch. 1, trans. Philip Yampolsky

q: The craftsman who works in silence is not ignoring the world. The craftsman who works in silence is listening to it.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Edward Brown

q: Do not seek fame in your work. Do not seek criticism either. Seek to do the work as well as it can be done. The rest will take care of itself.
s: Jātaka 240 (Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The teacher does not give wisdom; the teacher removes the obstacles to wisdom that the student has accumulated.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.63, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: What is the Dharma? Eat when hungry, sleep when tired, work when it is time to work. This is the practice of ten thousand teachers.
s: Sayings of Layman Pang (Pang Yun), trans. Ruth Fuller Sasaki

q: Layman Pang said: how wonderful! How wondrous! I chop wood; I carry water.
s: Sayings of Layman Pang (Pang Yun), trans. Ruth Fuller Sasaki

q: In the act of making, the maker and the made are not two different things. The act of making is the act of being made.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Uji (The Time Being), Dōgen Zenji, trans. David Loy

q: A meditator who does not sit is like a craftsman who keeps his tools oiled but never uses them. The oil is good; the tools must also be used.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.55 (Soṇa Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Even the most patient wood cannot be carved by a blunt chisel. Keep your tools sharp; keep your mind sharp.
s: Milindapañha 3.4.7, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: When asked how to purify the mind, the Buddha pointed to the sunrise. No word was needed. Purity was already demonstrated.
s: Udāna 3.10, trans. John Ireland

q: The ox and the cart travel the road together. Stopping the cart by striking the cart is foolish. To stop the cart, stop the ox.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 19 commentary (on training the mind, not the circumstance), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: All that we are is the result of what we have thought. The mind is everything. What we think, we become.
s: Dhammapada 1.1, commentary rendering, trans. Thomas Byrom

q: In building, the measure comes first. In practice, the intention comes first. A well-set intention is the measure by which all practice is built.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 2 (Sabbāsava Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The truly patient one is not one who endures without complaint, but one who endures while the mind remains clear and undistorted.
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.14, Śāntideva, trans. Kate Crosby

q: There is something that was here before any hammer struck, before any needle was threaded, before any seed was planted. Find that. Everything else follows from finding that.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 1, trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: The one who works slowly and well has more to show at the end of a year than the one who works quickly and carelessly.
s: Jātaka 355 (Uraga Jātaka), verse 3, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Said to be the last thing the great Tsongkhapa told his students before he died: 'Now I am going. Go practice; don't waste this human birth.'
s: Tsongkhapa, death scene account, traditional (Lam Rim tradition)

q: In the dark, feeling for a joint with your fingers, you know more than you know. Your hands have learned what your eyes cannot see.
s: Milindapañha 6.1.3, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: The rope around the post wears a groove. The thought returned to again and again wears a groove in the mind. Choose your grooves carefully.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 19 (Dvedhāvitakka Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Here, in this body of six feet, I declare, is the cosmos, its arising, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.45 (Rohitassa Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: To cross to the other shore of the river, a raft is needed. But a raft made of poor material will sink mid-stream. The precepts are the quality of the material.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.15, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Do not make a weapon of the Dharma; do not make a refuge of your cleverness. Both are traps disguised as tools.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 22 (Alagaddūpama Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Whatever is begun with a steady hand and a clear eye will find its completion in its own time. Do not force the completion.
s: Jātaka 469 (Mahāmora Jātaka), verse 8, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Teach generously; teach without reservation. The lamp is not less for having lit others.
s: Jātaka 540 (Sāma Jātaka), verse 14, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Every piece made is a teacher for the next piece. Every sitting is a teacher for the next sitting. Bring the teaching forward.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Bendōwa, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: The nail driven by a confident hand holds. The nail driven by a hesitant hand works loose. Find the confidence — not the confidence that you will succeed, but that the work is worth doing.
s: Jātaka 407 (Kaṭṭhabharī Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: When the task is done, step back. The space you leave around finished work lets others see it clearly.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Thomas Wright

q: In a forest, the tallest tree is the first to be struck by lightning. Be excellent without being conspicuous. This is the teaching of the forest.
s: Jātaka 310 (Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The Blessed One spent six years in ascetic practice before finding the Middle Way. The Middle Way is not found by reading about it; it is found by going past both extremes.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 36 (Mahāsaccaka Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Whatever is grasped with a tense hand breaks. Whatever is held with a gentle hand stays. Practice with attention but without grasping.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.55 (Soṇa Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The mind of a child — open, curious, undefended — is closer to the Buddha-mind than the mind of a learned scholar.
s: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Weatherhill

q: The sage sees both the nail and the space around it. It is the space that allows the nail to be what it is.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Sansuikyō, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Carl Bielefeldt

q: When a craftsman says 'I made this,' something is both true and false. True: the hands moved. False: the hands moved alone.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.37 (Natumha Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Before the board was shaped, it was a tree. Before it was a tree, it was a seed. Before it was a seed — where was it? That is the question you should carry into the workshop.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 2, commentary, trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: Whatever you make, you also unmake — because you have taken it from the world and returned it changed. The craftsman is responsible for this exchange.
s: Jātaka 190 (Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka), verse 7, trans. H.T. Francis

q: There is a kind of care that comes only from love — not the love of the self, but the love of the work. This care cannot be faked.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Edward Brown

q: The dharma gate has no door. Everyone can enter; no one is kept out. The only barrier is the one you bring with you.
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Prologue, trans. Robert Aitken

q: The master calligrapher does not think about the brush; the brush thinks about the paper. The master carpenter does not think about the chisel; the chisel thinks about the wood.
s: Zen art tradition (zenga), attributed to Hakuin Ekaku, traditional commentary

q: Forty years in the workshop, and I am still a beginner. This is not discouraging — this is the good news.
s: Jātaka 480 (Bhuridatta Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Knowing the whole requires knowing each part. Knowing each part requires knowing the whole. The craftsman lives in this circle every day.
s: Avataṃsaka Sūtra (Flower Garland Sutra), ch. 34, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Asked how long one must train, the master said: 'As long as there is something left to do.' Asked when that would end, the master said: 'When you stop asking.'
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 84, commentary, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: The truly skilled do not show off their skill. The truly wise do not parade their wisdom. You will find them in ordinary places, doing ordinary things, extraordinarily well.
s: Jātaka 316 (Mahāumagga Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Even a short life, fully and well lived, is complete. Even a long life, carelessly lived, is incomplete.
s: Dhammapada 8.111, commentary, trans. Narada Thera

q: The teacher who uses only words to teach carpentry has not taught carpentry. The teacher who teaches only by example has come closer. The teacher who teaches while the student's hands move — that one has taught.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.155, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: In the morning, before beginning, look at your tools. Are they ready? Then look at your mind. Is it ready? Then begin.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, opening commentary, trans. Thomas Wright

q: To make something beautiful requires a beautiful intention. The intention is the invisible ingredient that cannot be supplied by skill alone.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.40, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The greatest teachers are always also students. The greatest craftsmen are always also apprentices. Humility keeps the hands open.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.151, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Do not be in a hurry to teach what you have learned. First, let it settle into you. What has settled cannot be dislodged by questions.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 21 (Kakacūpama Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The work exists in the middle space between the worker and the world. Neither alone produces it.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.15, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Asked: 'What is your daily practice?' The master said: 'When I am cold, I look for fire. When I am hungry, I look for rice.' Nothing was left out of this answer.
s: Recorded Sayings of the Chan Masters (Zutangji), vol. 6, trans. Albert Welter

q: A monk asked: 'How do I not fall into cause and effect?' The master said: 'You cannot avoid cause and effect.' The monk was enlightened.
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 2, trans. Robert Aitken

q: The teaching of co-arising says: because this is, that is; because this ceases, that ceases. Every material participates in this — the nail knows the wood; the wood knows the nail.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 38 (Mahātaṇhāsankhaya Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The meditator learns to be interested in what is actually here, rather than what ought to be here. This is the practice of honesty applied to experience.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: A practitioner must be like good timber: seasoned, stable, responsive to the tools of the teaching, not green and full of resistance.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.100, commentary (Paṃsudhovaka Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: When you pick up the tool with the right mind, the tool does the work. When you pick it up with the wrong mind, you fight the tool all day.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: To study the Buddha-way is to study the self. But once found, the self is no longer an obstacle.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Asked what the Dharma was, Zhaozhou said: 'Your everyday mind.' Asked what the everyday mind was, he said: 'When you're hungry, eat. When you're tired, sleep. When you're cold, get warm.'
s: Sayings of Zhaozhou (Zhaozhoulu), trans. James Green

q: Every material has its nature. Work with its nature, and it will do more than you ask. Work against its nature, and it will teach you a painful lesson.
s: Milindapañha 5.1.3, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: The mark of mastery: the finished piece does not look worked; it looks inevitable. As if it could not have been otherwise.
s: Jātaka 222 (Kiṃpakka Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Even in the last moment of dying, the untrained mind grasps. Practice is practice for that moment. Do not wait until then to begin.
s: Bardo Tödröl (Tibetan Book of the Dead), ch. 1, trans. Chogyam Trungpa

q: The first sound of the hammer in the morning is a teaching. The last sound at dusk is also a teaching. What is being taught?
s: Dōgen Zenji, Eihei Kōroku, vol. 7, trans. Taigen Dan Leighton

q: When the mind is like an open sky, nothing that passes through it leaves a mark. When the mind is like a closed room, everything that passes through it leaves a residue.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Zazenshin, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: In the end, what you have made is not for you. What you have practiced is not for you. All of this was offered into the stream. That is the gift.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 135 (Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: On a cold night, the fire welcomes everyone equally. The sun rises on the just and unjust alike. This is the teacher of compassion without discrimination.
s: Itivuttaka 27, trans. John Ireland

q: He who has truly seen impermanence does not need to be told to work diligently. Urgency arises naturally from that seeing.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.20, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Sitting, the meditator is like a mountain — heavy, stable, unmoving, not easily disturbed by what passes around it.
