s: Majjhima Nikāya 119 (Kāyagatāsati Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: A bucket dropped into a well comes back full. A mind turned toward the Dhamma comes back full.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.1, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The one who quarrels with materials is not yet a craftsman. First, learn to work with what is before you — not what you wish were before you.
s: Jātaka 33 (Sammā-paribbājanīya Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The best day's work is work you cannot remember because your hands knew what to do without consulting you.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Thomas Wright

q: A mind that is quick to blame the tool has not yet understood the hand.
s: Milindapañha 4.1.3, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: The one who learns only from success learns half of what there is to know. The other half comes only from failure.
s: Jātaka 150 (Sañjīva Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: It is said that Ānanda remembered every word the Buddha ever spoke. But remembering is not the same as knowing. The one who puts a single word into practice knows more than the one who remembers ten thousand.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.102, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Asked how to cultivate patience, the master said: 'Find the thing that tests it most, and go there every day.'
s: Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.2, Śāntideva, commentary tradition, trans. Kate Crosby

q: When you do not know, say you do not know. This honesty is the foundation of all genuine learning.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 58 (Abhayarājakumāra Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The one who wastes no material wastes no mind. The one who wastes no mind wastes no time. The one who wastes no time wastes no life.
s: Jātaka 269 (Sattubhasta Jātaka), commentary, trans. Robert Chalmers

q: What you give to the fire, the fire transforms. What you give to the teacher, the teacher transforms. What you give to the practice, the practice transforms. Give generously to all three.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.66 (Kālāma Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Sāriputta was asked: 'What does the noble disciple give up?' He said: 'Stinginess, ill-will, wrong view — one by one, like a craftsman who removes the flaws before presenting the finished piece.'
s: Majjhima Nikāya 24 (Rathavinīta Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Walking slowly, one sees more than walking quickly. Thinking slowly, one understands more than thinking quickly. Work at the pace of understanding.
s: Dīgha Nikāya 22 (Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta), commentary, trans. Maurice Walshe

q: Linji shouted. Deshan struck. These were not rude behaviors — they were precise instruments, applied with great skill to break a precisely identified obstacle.
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 32, commentary, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: The cypress tree stands in the courtyard in rain and in sun, in spring and in frost. It does not explain itself. Neither should the practice.
s: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), Case 37, commentary, trans. Kōun Yamada

q: A Jātaka tale asks: what tool is sharpest? The answer given is: the mind that wants to learn.
s: Jātaka 336 (Kumbhakāra Jātaka), verse 4, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The path is walked one step at a time. The path is walked one step at a time. The path is walked one step at a time. This is not a repetition — this is the instruction.
s: Samyutta Nikāya 45.8, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Long is the night for one who lies awake. Long is the road for one who is weary. Long is samsara for the fool who does not know the true Dhamma.
s: Dhammapada 5.60, trans. Narada Thera

q: The Blessed One said: I do not dispute with the world. It is the world that disputes with me. One who knows the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.94 (Puppha Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: As a silversmith purifies silver — step by step, blow by blow, not all at once — so the meditator purifies the mind.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 39 (Mahā-Assapura Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: What cannot be said by words is not hidden. It is open, visible, present — but only to one who has stopped talking long enough to look.
s: Vimalakīrti Sūtra, ch. 9, commentary, trans. Robert Thurman

q: Asked about Zen, Nanquan cut the cat in two. Asked about the right response, Zhaozhou put his sandal on his head. Neither answer can be argued with.
s: Blue Cliff Record, Case 63, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: Whatever is practiced regularly becomes natural. Whatever becomes natural requires no effort. Effort, applied consistently, dissolves itself.
s: Visuddhimagga IV.1, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: In the workshop of the mind, craving is the apprentice who keeps changing the blueprint. The master must teach the apprentice to be still.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 38 (Mahātaṇhāsankhaya Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The Dharma is not a doctrine; it is a direction. It points toward freedom. Do not stop at the pointing finger and say you have arrived.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 3, trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: Silence is not empty. It is full of answers to questions you have not yet learned to ask.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Butsukōjōji (Going Beyond Buddha), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Vimalakirti was ill. Manjushri asked how he bore it. Vimalakirti said: 'From foolishness comes existence; from existence comes illness. I bear it as a physician bears the illnesses of those he treats.'
s: Vimalakīrti Sūtra, ch. 5, trans. Burton Watson

q: The monk who repairs his robe, stitch by careful stitch, is doing the same work as the monk who repairs his mind, moment by careful moment.
s: Vinaya Piṭaka, Mahāvagga VIII.3, trans. I.B. Horner

q: To make the impermanent look permanent is vanity. To make the impermanent look beautiful while knowing it is impermanent — this is art.
s: Jātaka 151 (Kurudhamma Jātaka), commentary, trans. H.T. Francis

q: The teacher who is in a hurry to see results has forgotten why the teaching exists.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.155, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: A question asked with a truly open mind changes the one who asks it, before any answer arrives.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 63 (Cūḷamāluṅkya Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The bamboo grove does not force itself to be beautiful. It grows according to its nature and is beautiful because of that.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Sansuikyō, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Carl Bielefeldt

q: Entering the forest does not make you a forest person. Living in the forest, season after season, year after year — that makes you a forest person. So too, entering practice.
s: Theragāthā 2.2 (Nāgasamāla Thera), commentary, trans. K.R. Norman

q: When you make something and it does not work, the thing that did not work is teaching you what must come next. Listen to it.
s: Jātaka 175 (Āsaṅka Jātaka), verse 5, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The finest joint is invisible. The finest teaching leaves no trace. The finest action leaves no residue. This is the perfection of craft.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Edward Brown

q: What takes one day to learn takes ten years to do well. There is no gap between learning and practice — only the gap you create by separating them.
s: Milindapañha 2.1.7, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: All rivers run to the sea, yet the sea is not full. All effort flows into the practice, yet practice is never exhausted.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 26 (Ariyapariyesanā Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Nagarjuna's student asked: 'If everything is empty, what is there to practice?' He said: 'Everything.'
s: Vigrahavyāvartanī (The Rebuttal of Objections), Nāgārjuna, commentary tradition, trans. Jan Westerhoff

q: The instruction says: sit as if you will never rise again. Rise as if you have never sat. This is how to do one thing completely.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Zazenshin, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Even the Buddha took rest. Even the great teachers stopped. Knowing when to stop is not weakness; it is the craft of sustainable effort.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.16, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: One sila kept perfectly is worth more than a thousand precepts memorized and broken.
s: Visuddhimagga I.19, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The forest is full of tools that were never picked up. The earth is full of seeds that were never planted. Begin — this is the rarest act.
s: Jātaka 510 (Mahājanaka Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: Do not mistake the reflection of the moon in the water for the moon itself. Do not mistake the description of the Dharma for the Dharma itself.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 2, trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: The master builder said: the house is not made of wood and stone; it is made of the will that chose each piece of wood and each stone.
s: Jātaka 407 (Kaṭṭhabharī Jātaka), verse 6, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Practice does not erase the person; it clarifies the person until the essential nature shines through, like gold purified of dross.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.100 (Paṃsudhovaka Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Whatever you are doing now, do it as if it were the most important thing in the world. When it is done, let it go, and do the next thing as if that were the most important thing.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Thomas Wright

q: The ancient craftsmen did not sign their work. They knew: the work would speak, or it would not. Their humility was their signature.
s: Jātaka 222 (Kiṃpakka Jātaka), verse 3, trans. H.T. Francis

q: Even the bell is silent until it is struck. Even the greatest teaching is silent until a student strikes it with a sincere question.
s: Dōgen Zenji, Eihei Kōroku, vol. 2, trans. Taigen Dan Leighton

q: Rinzai said: the student who seeks the Dharma outside will never find it. It is not in the east, not in the west, not above, not below. It is right here, always was.
s: Record of Linji (Línjì Yùlù), trans. Burton Watson

q: Said Mahākassapa: 'I have made my bed under the open sky for forty years. The sky has not once failed me as a roof.'
s: Theragāthā 18.1, commentary, trans. K.R. Norman

q: The calligrapher who has written ten thousand characters knows something the one who has written one hundred does not: that the brush leads, and the hand follows.
s: Zen art tradition (zenga), Hakuin Ekaku, commentary

q: Whatever is finished reveals what could not be seen while it was being made. This is why masters examine finished work with the eyes of a stranger.
s: Jātaka 316 (Mahāumagga Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The saw that is drawn too hard loses its teeth. The mind that is pressed too hard loses its edge. The middle tension is the only tension that holds.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.55 (Soṇa Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Asked why he kept sweeping leaves in autumn, knowing more would fall, the monk said: 'That is exactly why I keep sweeping.'
s: Zen teaching story, traditional (Rinzai lineage)

q: The Buddhadharma does not belong to India, or China, or Japan. It belongs to whoever practices it completely, wherever they are.
s: Dōgen Zenji, Eihei Kōroku, vol. 9, trans. Taigen Dan Leighton

q: Do not correct the student's hand until you have understood what their hand is trying to do. Then the correction is received as help, not as criticism.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.155, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The potter's wheel turns; the clay rises; the bowl appears. Where was the bowl before? The answer is the same as the answer to: where were you before you were born?
s: Zen kōan tradition, attributed to Guishan Lingyou, traditional

q: The finest work comes from the meeting of skill and stillness. Skill without stillness is agitation. Stillness without skill is inertia.
s: Visuddhimagga IV.49, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: When Bodhidharma first came to China, he sat facing a wall for nine years. Those nine years were not wasted — they were the teaching.
s: Zutangji (Patriarchs' Hall Collection), trans. Albert Welter

q: What has been bent by habit can be straightened by practice. What has been straightened by practice becomes the new habit. This is how the mind is made.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 19 (Dvedhāvitakka Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The tree does not know it is making shade. The practice does not know it is making peace. This is how the deepest benefits are conferred.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Robert Aitken

q: The Dharma is not a comfort; it is a compass. Comfort tells you what you want to hear; a compass tells you where you are.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 26 (Ariyapariyesanā Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: At the moment of first sight, the eye and the seen are one. Between that moment and the story you tell about it — there is where suffering is born.
s: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.95 (Dvayaṃ Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: The knife does not cut itself. The eye does not see itself. The mind does not know itself — except in the rare moment when practice turns it around.
s: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, ch. 2, trans. D.T. Suzuki

q: Whatever is done carelessly must be done again. Whatever is done well need not be done again. A life of careful work is a life of less work.
s: Jātaka 178 (Daddara Jātaka), verse 7, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The one who has learned to wait without anxiety has learned one of the hardest skills there is — and one of the most useful.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.28, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: Even the sun sets. Even the teaching ends. Even the greatest master falls silent. Everything complete becomes a beginning.
s: Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16), closing verse, trans. Maurice Walshe

q: After finishing, clean your tools. After sitting, bow. After speaking, listen. After giving, let go. This completes each act.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Asked about death, Dōgen said: 'Flowers fall and weeds spread. This is what I can tell you.' Nothing was left unsaid.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Shōji (Birth and Death), Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Norman Waddell

q: The eye that has seen the nature of things does not unsee it. You can forget many things; you cannot forget this. This is why it is called liberation.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 36 (Mahāsaccaka Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: Whatever is built on sand will not stand. Whatever is built on rock will stand until it is deliberately torn down. The precepts are the rock.
s: Visuddhimagga I.1 (opening verse commentary), trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: There is a kind of tiredness that comes from work well done — it is different in quality from the tiredness of worry. The first is restorative; the second is not.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 4 (Bhayabherava Sutta), commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli

q: The teaching comes alive when it meets the life of the student. Before that meeting, it is only words.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.68, commentary, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi

q: What is complete needs nothing added. What is empty needs nothing removed. The sage's work is to know the difference.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Genjōkōan, Dōgen Zenji, commentary, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: Asked what dharma he taught, Mazu said: 'No dharma at all.' Asked what practice he recommended, he said: 'Sitting, just sitting.' The student was puzzled for thirty years, then understood both answers at once.
s: Extensive Record of Mazu Daoyi (Mazu Daoyi Chanshi Yulu), trans. Cheng Chien Bhikshu

q: The practice of a lifetime is this: to be fully where you are, with what you have, doing what is needed, without complaint and without praise.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, concluding commentary, trans. Thomas Wright

q: The oil lamp does not hesitate before giving light. The compassionate person does not hesitate before giving help. This is the teaching of the lamp.
s: Itivuttaka 26, commentary, trans. John Ireland

q: Whatever you carry with you into the workshop — worry, pride, distraction — you will find it in the work when you are done. Leave it at the door.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Edward Brown

q: The ancient ones made their robes from discarded cloth. They chose difficulty not from poverty but from wisdom: what is hard to obtain is carefully kept.
s: Vinaya Piṭaka, Mahāvagga VIII.1, trans. I.B. Horner

q: In Zen, poverty is honored: the bowl with one chip, the robe with one patch, the hut with one window facing east. What is enough is more than enough.
s: Dōgen Zenji, Eihei Kōroku, vol. 4, trans. Taigen Dan Leighton

q: The teaching does not run out. The practice does not run out. The need does not run out. Only the day runs out — which is why we begin again tomorrow.
s: Majjhima Nikāya 131 (Bhaddekaratta Sutta), commentary, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu

q: After the great flood subsides, the land left behind is richer than before. After the great difficulty, the mind left standing is deeper than before.
s: Jātaka 522 (Samuddavāṇija Jātaka), commentary, trans. E.B. Cowell

q: The hammer strikes the same spot a thousand times. The thousandth strike is no different from the first — and yet, after the thousandth, the nail is home.
s: Milindapañha 3.4.2, trans. T.W. Rhys Davids

q: The student asked: 'How do I know when the practice is right?' The master said: 'Ask the work, not the practitioner.'
s: Book of Serenity, Case 89, commentary, trans. Thomas Cleary

q: What is made with the whole body, the whole mind, and the whole heart — that thing carries something that cannot be added afterward. Give everything now.
s: Tenzo Kyōkun, Dōgen Zenji, trans. Shohaku Okumura

q: The sun rises every day on a world that has never existed before. You rise every day as a person who has never existed before. This is not a small thing.
s: Shōbōgenzō: Uji (The Time Being), Dōgen Zenji, trans. Norman Waddell

q: When the student has gone beyond the teacher, the teacher is pleased. When the student has gone beyond the teaching, the teaching is fulfilled.
s: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.159, trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi
